prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view of a circular dining table directly in front of and below the camera wearer (0.4–0.9 m away), surrounded by a person in beige on the bottom left (~0.5–0.8 m), a man in a grey shirt on the upper right (~0.9–1.2 m, about 1.0 m across from the left diner), and three background diners further up-left (1.3–2.2 m away). In frames 1–3, a standing person's outstretched right arm enters from the right edge at very close range (~0.3–0.5 m, bright white) above the right edge of the table to pick up a mason jar and clear a dirty plate, while by frame 5 the camera turns slightly right as the camera wearer's own two hands rise into the foreground (~0.25–0.35 m) within immediate arm's reach of the table's utensils, plates, and bowls. The map clearly separates the depth layering of overlapping limbs, standing menus, bottles, and the tilted tabletop gradient better than the cluttered RGB image alone. However, it is unreliable on transparent or reflective tableware—such as the glass sundae goblet, empty jars, and flat utensils—which blend into the table surface, and it loses facial detail so it cannot independently show that the seated diners are facing inward toward the table and looking down at their phones or food rather than at the camera wearer.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map labels the central dining table (0.4–0.9 m away) and localizes the tabletop items within arm's reach of the camera wearer and seated neighbors, including bottles and upright menus on the upper-left (~0.7–0.9 m), a napkin holder labeled as a bowl in the center (~0.6 m), a fork and knife on the lower-right (~0.5 m), and a sundae in a wine glass near the top-right edge (~0.8 m). Around the table's perimeter, it segments the seated person in beige on the bottom left (~0.5–0.8 m, facing right), the grey-shirted man on the upper right (~1.0 m, facing left toward the table and holding a cell phone segmented in frames 4–5), background diners ~1.2–2.0 m to the upper left, and the server's reaching arm on the right (~0.3–0.5 m) in frames 1–3. Across the five frames, the masks track the mason jar (labeled as a cup in frame 1 and wine glass in frame 2) moving right as it is lifted off the table, followed by the camera wearer's own arms and hands entering the bottom-right foreground (~0.3 m) in frames 3–5 as the viewpoint shifts rightward. While segmentation isolates small overlapping objects like the cell phone, utensils, and glassware from the dark tabletop, it is noisy and inconsistent across frames—leaving large unsegmented black gaps on the food plates, misclassifying the napkin holder as a bowl and a blue trash bin on the far right (~1.8 m) as a bottle in frame 5, and merging or fragmenting partially occluded people at the frame boundaries.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is mostly blank black and fails to detect any full-body skeletons (yellow) for the five people seated around the table (ranging from 0.5 m to 2.0 m away) or the person reaching in from the right, because everyone is heavily occluded by the table and cropped by the steep downward camera angle. Instead, it only renders isolated 3D hand skeletons (magenta) in frames 1, 3, and 5: the server's right hand (~0.4 m away) reaching down from the right over a plate and another hand at the bottom-right holding that plate's rim (~0.4 m) in frame 1; the grey-shirted man's two hands (~0.9 m away, ~0.1 m apart) holding a phone on the upper right and the server's retreating right hand (~0.5 m) below them in frame 3; and the camera wearer's own left and right hands (~0.3 m away, touching at the fingertips) raised in the lower-right foreground in frame 5. When present, these wireframes reveal precise finger articulation, palm orientation, and pinch posture—such as the downward five-finger grasp in frame 1 and the bimanual fingertip contact in frame 5—more clearly than the motion-blurred RGB frames. However, the pose map is highly unreliable overall, completely missing all hands in frames 2 and 4 (including the blurry hand lifting the jar and hands resting on the left side of the table) and providing no information about head orientation, gaze direction, or scene layout.
